note: Nestor#17 asked for asymmetric seal signatures and, in doing so, forced a positioning decision it named explicitly: where does the signing happen. The server-side half shipped in 6ca5a5e (ed25519 behind the [keys] extra, verify-without-forge proven across two instances). This records the decisions that shipping made and the one it deliberately left open, because the issue's own framing is that the crypto swap is the easy part and the where-does-the-key-live question is the real one. Filed when the QUESTIONS §6 and README import-table prose were reconciled to the shipped state — the docs had gone on saying the asymmetric half was 'still missing' after it landed, which is the §6.92 drift shape one more time.

decisions.question: Asymmetric signing needs a library the stdlib does not have. Does that cost the zero-dependency guarantee?
decisions.commitment: No. It lives behind a [keys] optional extra (cryptography>=41). HMAC stays the default, the core stays dependency-free, and an ed25519 keyring without the extra refuses loudly at BOTH sign and verify.
decisions.why: Zero runtime dependencies is load-bearing here — it is in the README, it is QUESTIONS §16, and it is why nestor.ui is http.server plus one inlined page. Checked, not assumed: hashlib offers no Ed25519 and ssl exposes no signing API, so this genuinely needs cryptography or PyNaCl, and rolling our own is not a discussion. The extra is the same shape [cloud] already uses to gate anthropic, so the pattern was already blessed. The one non-obvious call is that a missing extra must refuse, never degrade: a seal that silently fell back to unsigned because a dependency was absent would be the Nestor#2 forgery with an ImportError as its accomplice. So _load_ed25519 raises SigningRequiredError at both ends, and the refusal is tested by simulating the missing dependency rather than requiring a second environment.

decisions.question: Where does the private key live — the server, or the verifier's own device?
decisions.commitment: Server-side, for now. The instance that signs holds its verifiers' private keys; only public keys travel. Browser/client-side signing is deliberately left open as its own piece of work.
decisions.why: The issue's table has four cells; server-side ed25519 clears the one that matters for every cross-boundary use Nestor actually has. An instance holding only a peer's public key can verify that peer's seals and is structurally unable to produce one — so two instances, or two organisations, exchange verification capability without exchanging forgery capability, which is exactly what a shared HMAC could never give and what Q2 (import into a different instance) and Q8 (sync) need. What server-side signing does NOT close is the operator of the signing instance forging as anyone whose key lives there, because the process holds those private keys to sign with them. Closing that requires signing where the key lives — WebCrypto ed25519 in the browser, or a client-side agent — which turns signing._message from an internal detail into a wire contract between two implementations and is a UI architecture change with its own consequences. That is real work with a real interface-design cost, and bundling it into the crypto swap would have held the cross-instance win hostage to a browser rewrite. So it ships as its own decision, and the residual cell is stated honestly in QUESTIONS §6 rather than papered over.

decisions.question: A public-key keyring holds nothing secret. Does the 0600 permission refusal still apply to it?
decisions.commitment: The refusal follows the key MATERIAL, not the filename. Any hmac key, ed25519 private half, or legacy key still demands 0600; a public-only keyring is deliberately distributable.
decisions.why: keyring.load refusing a group/other-readable file is correct for a file that holds a signing secret and wrong for one that holds only public keys — the whole point of the asymmetric upgrade is a keyring you can commit, mirror into FRANK, and hand to the other side of an import. So the check computes holds_secrets (any non-ed25519 entry, any ed25519 entry carrying its private half, or a legacy_key) and only then demands the mode. A public-only keyring loads regardless of mode, and the error message says so, so nobody chmods a file that never needed it. The private half is also kept out of the distributed shape structurally: VerifierKey.to_json emits 'private' only when it is present, so a peer entry built from a public key alone cannot accidentally serialize a secret it does not have.

decisions.question: Rejections under an ed25519 verifier whose private half is not on this instance — refuse, or record unsigned?
decisions.commitment: Record unsigned, never refuse. A private-holder's rejection signs and verifies as before; a public-only holder's rejection is honored and reported unsigned.
decisions.why: Refusing to record a 'no' is the one direction rejection must never fail in — a refused rejection leaves a bad answer serving because the reviewer's key happened to live elsewhere. This is the same asymmetry memory.rejected_ids already documents (honoring a forged rejection only withholds an answer, which is Nestor's safe state), extended to the case where the verifier simply cannot sign here. Seals go the other way and MUST refuse a public-only signer, because serving an unbacked seal is the failure that direction cannot afford — and that split, seal-refuses / rejection-records, is the invariant the two-instance tests pin in both directions.
